lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7, how did binary search find a number? (It checked the middle, then threw away the half the number could not be in.) Today: comparing algorithms by counting their steps.
Two algorithms can solve the same problem in very different numbers of steps. Computer scientists compare them by counting steps in the worst case: the most steps the algorithm could ever need.
Linear search's worst case grows with the list: n items, n checks. Binary search's grows very slowly: double the list and it needs just one more check. For 64 items it needs 7 checks, not 64.
Bubble sort compares neighbours in passes. With every pass to the end, n items need n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons: 10 items need 45, but 100 items need 4,950.
Worked example: find a name in 1,000 sorted names. Linear search may need 1,000 checks; binary search needs at most 10. For a million names: a million checks against 20. The gap grows as lists grow.
Merge sort, from grade 7, splits and merges. For 1,000 items it needs fewer than 9,000 comparisons, while bubble sort's passes make 499,500. For big lists, a better algorithm beats a faster computer.
The best choice also depends on the job: a short list, a list searched only once, or code that must be simple to check. Simple algorithms are easier to write correctly. Choose the one that fits.
Try it in the world: find a word in a dictionary by opening it near the middle again and again, then by reading from the first page. Count the pages you look at. Next: models and abstraction.

exercises.prompt: A linear search looks through 50 unsorted names. What is the most checks it can need?
exercises.hint: In the worst case, where is the name?
exercises.explain: In the worst case the name is last or missing, so it checks all 50 names: 50 checks.

exercises.prompt: Which grows most slowly as the list gets longer?
exercises.explain: Binary search's line stays almost flat: doubling the list adds only one check.

exercises.prompt: Doubling a sorted list adds only one check to binary search's worst case.
exercises.hint: What does binary search's first check do to a list twice as long?
exercises.explain: True: the first check halves the doubled list back to the old size.

exercises.prompt: An algorithm's worst case is the fewest steps it can take.
exercises.explain: False: the worst case is the most steps it could ever need; the fewest is the best case.

exercises.prompt: Match each algorithm to its idea.
exercises.hint: Remember how each one moves through a list.
exercises.explain: Linear search checks in turn, binary search halves, bubble sort swaps neighbours and merge sort splits then merges.

exercises.prompt: Bubble sort sorts 8 items, every pass going to the end. How many comparisons? Use n × (n − 1) ÷ 2.
What is the most checks binary search needs for 16 sorted items?
exercises.hint: Halve 16 again and again until 1 is left, and count every check.
exercises.explain: What is left: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is 5 checks at most.

exercises.prompt: 6 unsorted items are searched once. Which is the better choice?
choices: binary search: it is always faster
exercises.hint: Think about the extra work sorting takes.
exercises.explain: Sorting first costs more than 6 checks, so a simple linear search wins on a short list searched once.

exercises.prompt: Order these from the fewest to the most steps for 100 items, in the worst case.
exercises.hint: Work out each one for n = 100.
exercises.explain: Binary search: 7 checks; linear search: 100; bubble sort: 100 × 99 ÷ 2 = 4,950 comparisons.

exercises.prompt: Does it need a sorted list, or does it work on any list?
exercises.hint: Does it throw away half the list on each step?
exercises.explain: Binary search and guessing the middle need the items in order; the others look at every item, so any list will do.

exercises.prompt: For 1,000 items, bubble sort's passes make 499,500 comparisons.
Merge sort and bubble sort both sort 1,000 items. Which makes fewer comparisons?
exercises.hint: Compare 499,500 with the number for merge sort.
exercises.explain: Merge sort needs fewer than 9,000 comparisons for 1,000 items; bubble sort's passes make 499,500.

exercises.prompt: Binary search needs at most 10 checks for 1,000 sorted items. At most how many for 2,000?
exercises.hint: What does one extra check do to the list?
exercises.explain: One check halves 2,000 to 1,000, then 10 more at most: 11 checks.

exercises.prompt: 1,000,000 sorted items: how many more checks can linear search need than binary search, at most?
exercises.hint: Work out each worst case first.
exercises.explain: Linear: 1,000,000 checks. Binary: 20 (2 to the power 20 is just over a million). 1,000,000 − 20 = 999,980.

exercises.prompt: Bubble sort makes 45 comparisons for 10 items. How many for 20 items?
exercises.explain: 20 × 19 = 380, and 380 ÷ 2 = 190: doubling the list makes about 4 times the work.

exercises.prompt: The algorithm that is fastest on huge lists is always the best choice.
exercises.hint: Think of short lists, data searched once and code that must be simple.
exercises.explain: False: for short or unsorted lists, or code that must be simple to check, a simpler algorithm can be the better choice.

exercises.prompt: Program the robot to the flag in as few commands as you can.
exercises.hint: Plan the route on the board before you start: each turn costs a command too.
exercises.explain: A shortest program: FORWARD, FORWARD, FORWARD, TURN RIGHT, FORWARD, FORWARD, FORWARD, FORWARD, 8 commands. Like a good algorithm, the best route does the job in the fewest steps.

exercises.prompt: Pick up the gem, then reach the flag, in as few commands as you can.
exercises.hint: Find the gem's best route first, then the flag's: count turns as well as moves.
exercises.explain: A shortest program: FORWARD, TURN RIGHT, FORWARD, FORWARD, TURN LEFT, FORWARD, FORWARD, FORWARD, TURN RIGHT, FORWARD, FORWARD, 11 commands. Comparing routes is comparing algorithms: both work, but one takes fewer steps.

exercises.prompt: Order these sorted lists by binary search's most checks, fewest first.
exercises.hint: Each check halves what is left.
exercises.explain: At most 4 checks for 15, 7 for 100, 10 for 1,000 and 20 for 1,000,000.
